events.title: Chromebooks go on sale
events.summary: Samsung and Acer put the first retail Chromebooks on sale on June 15, 2011 — consumer laptops running Chrome [OS] after Google announced them at I/O on May 11.
events.about: After the CR-48 pilot, retail Chromebooks brought Google's browser-centric [OS] to schools and budget buyers — automatic updates, Google account sign-in, and web apps only. [IT] departments adopted them for managed classrooms; developers tested PWAs and Chrome extensions on locked-down hardware. The category grew into a major segment beside Windows and Mac laptops.

narrative.whyChosen: Retail Chromebooks turned Google's pilot into a shipping product category.
narrative.whyImportant: They proved cloud-first laptops could sell beyond beta testers and education pilots.
narrative.problemSolved: Consumers and schools needed affordable laptops with zero-maintenance software updates.

events.title: Laravel first beta released
events.summary: Taylor Otwell released the first Laravel beta on June 9, 2011 — a PHP web framework emphasizing elegant syntax and developer ergonomics.
events.about: Laravel brought routing, Eloquent ORM, and Blade templates to PHP with conventions inspired by Ruby on Rails. It grew into the most popular PHP framework for APIs and full-stack apps — artisan [CLI], queues, and later Livewire and Forge hosting.

narrative.whyChosen: Laravel redefined modern PHP web development with expressive APIs and strong conventions.
narrative.whyImportant: It made PHP competitive for new web projects when Rails and Django dominated mindshare.
narrative.problemSolved: PHP frameworks lacked cohesive ergonomics; developers wanted Rails-like productivity on PHP.

events.title: Firefox 5 released
events.summary: [Mozilla] released [Firefox] 5 on June 21, 2011 — the first version on the rapid release schedule with faster update cadence.
events.about: [Firefox] 5 shipped Do Not Track headers and [CSS] animation improvements as [Mozilla] moved to six-week release cycles like Chrome. Web developers tested against fresher browser versions but faced faster breaking changes in vendor prefixes and APIs.

narrative.whyChosen: [Firefox] 5 kicked off [Mozilla]'s rapid release model matching Chrome's pace.
narrative.whyImportant: It accelerated how quickly web platform features reached users — for better and worse.
narrative.problemSolved: Year-long [Firefox] releases left users waiting for security fixes and new web APIs.

events.title: CSS 2.1 becomes a W3C Recommendation
events.summary: The [W3C] published CSS Level 2 Revision 1 as a Recommendation on June 7, 2011 — a corrected, interoperable snapshot of CSS2 after fifteen years of refinement.
events.about: CSS 2.1 removed unimplementable CSS2 features, fixed specification errors, and reflected what browsers actually supported — backed by tens of thousands of test cases. It became the stable baseline the CSS Working Group built modular Level 3 specs on top of: selectors, flexbox, grid, and animations all trace back to this foundation.

narrative.whyChosen: CSS 2.1 ended years of spec drift and gave the web a stable styling baseline.
narrative.whyImportant: It unlocked modular CSS3 development by freezing a reliable interoperability target.
narrative.problemSolved: CSS2 contained errors and features no browser could implement consistently.
